title: Mutable state and the wire
dek: Git's objects never change, so they need no lock. Everything around them does change: the index, the refs, the reflogs, and the conversation between two repositories. This part reads those small mutable files and the wire protocol from git v2.55.0: the index as a stat cache that becomes a tree, racy git, what a reader sees while refs move, reftable's one-rename commit, why every publish is atomic but nothing is fsynced by default, pkt-lines and protocol v2, negotiation, and the push quarantine.
byline: 23 October 2026 · Subject: git@e9019fca (v2.55.0) · Part 2 of 3 · Read from the source and the manual; measured on this machine
description: Git's mutable state and transport, read from the git 2.55 source: the index format and racy git, lock timeouts, refs and reftable, atomic-but-not-durable publishing, pkt-lines and protocol v2, fetch negotiation and the push quarantine. Part 2 of Git, taken apart.
og_description: Part 2 of Git, taken apart. The index (a 62-byte stat record per path, a TREE cache, racy-git smudging), the 0/100/1000 ms lock policies, files vs reftable under a concurrent reader, the fsync defaults, pkt-line bytes, why protocol v2 saves bytes only through ref-prefix, negotiation rounds, and how a push sits in quarantine until pre-receive accepts it.
twitter_description: Git's index, refs, reftable, fsync defaults and wire protocol, read from v2.55.0 and measured. Part 2 of Git, taken apart.
badges_callout:
How to read the badges

from the code marks a fact read from git at e9019fca (tag v2.55.0, 29 June 2026), cited as a path and line number from the repository root; the manual pages are cited under Documentation/. measured here marks a number, byte dump or behaviour observed with git version 2.55.0 on a 2-vCPU Linux box; each says which script in ~/git-ref/lab/ produced it. reconstruction marks a judgement I drew from those sources rather than read in one place.

This is Part 2 of 3 of Git, taken apart. Part 1 covers the commit and its objects; Part 3 covers merging, upkeep and history.
